In total, 331 simultaneous meteors were detected across the two observation campaigns - 145 in ICCD09 and 228 in KISO18.
The relationship between radar cross section and optical V-band magnitude was well approximated by a linear function.
A transformation function was derived to convert radar cross section to V-band magnitude for sporadic meteors.

The luminosity function derived from about 150,000 meteors detected by the MU radar from 2009-2015 was well approximated by a single power-law function with a population index of 3.52 ± 0.12 in the magnitude range of -1.5 to 9.5 mag.
The present observations indicate that the MU radar has the capability to detect interplanetary dust in the mass range of about 10^-5 to 10^0 g as meteors.

The meteors detected in KISO18 were typically about 1.8 mag fainter than those in ICCD09, despite the larger distance between the radar and optical observation sites, due to the higher sensitivity of the Tomo-e Gozen camera.

The altitudes of the simultaneously detected meteors ranged from about 100-120 km, with the KISO18 meteors generally detected at lower altitudes than the ICCD09 meteors due to the displaced pointing of the Kiso telescope.

The luminosity function was derived by applying the transformation function from radar cross section to optical magnitude to about 150,000 meteors detected by the MU radar from 2009-2015, after removing contributions from known meteor showers.

Simultaneous radar and optical observations are important to constrain the physical parameters governing meteor brightness, such as the luminous efficiency and ionization coefficient, which are key to understanding the size distribution of interplanetary dust.

The derived optical magnitudes could be affected by unknown spectral characteristics of the meteors, as the color term correction was not applied, potentially introducing systematic biases in the relationship between radar cross section and optical magnitude.
About 20% of the meteors in ICCD09 showed light bursts with amplitudes larger than 1.5 mag in their light curves, possibly attributed to fragmentation.
The brightest meteor in ICCD09 was 1.4 mag, while the faintest was 10.0 mag. The magnitudes at 25-, 50-, and 75-percentiles were 5.0, 6.1, and 7.2 mag, respectively.
The brightest meteor in KISO18 was about 2.8 mag, while the faintest was 11.1 mag. The magnitudes at 25-, 50-, and 75-percentiles were 7.4, 8.1, and 8.6 mag, respectively.
The pointing of the Tomo-e Gozen telescope in KISO18 was slightly displaced, resulting in some simultaneous meteors having incomplete optical trajectories compared to the radar observations.
Contributions from known meteor showers were removed from the MU radar meteor archive based on the D-criterion, with a threshold of 0.2.
